# Proof of Schur's Theorem

David H. Wagner

dhwagnertx@mac.com

In this note, I provide more detail for the proof of Schur's Theorem found in Strang's Introduction to Linear Algebra[1]

Theorem 1. If A is a square real matrix with real eigenvalues, then there is an orthogonal matrix Q and an upper triangular matrix T such that $A=Q T Q^{\mathrm{T}}.$

Proof. Note that $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q T Q}^{\mathrm{T}} \Leftrightarrow \mathbf{A Q}=\mathbf{Q T}$ . Let $q_{1}$ be an eigenvector of norm 1, with eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}$ . Let $q_{2},\dots,q_{n}$ be any orthonormal vectors orthogonal to $q_{1}$ . Let $Q_{1}=[q_{1},\dots,q_{n}]$ . Then $Q_{1}^{\mathrm{T}}Q_{1}=\mathbf{I}$ , and

$$
\boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm {T}} \boldsymbol {A} \boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & \dots \\ \underline {{0}} & \boldsymbol {A} _ {2} \end{array} \right)
$$

(1)

Now I claim that $A_{2}$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_{2},\dots,\lambda_{n}.$ This is true because

Now I claim that $A_{2}$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_{2},\dots,\lambda_{n}.$ This is true because

$$
\begin{array}{l} \det (\boldsymbol {A} - \lambda \boldsymbol {I}) = \det \boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm {T}} \det (\boldsymbol {A} - \lambda \boldsymbol {I}) \det \boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} = \det \left(\boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm {T}} (\boldsymbol {A} - \lambda \boldsymbol {I}) \boldsymbol {Q} _ {1}\right) \\ = \det \left(\boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm {T}} \boldsymbol {A} \boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} - \lambda \boldsymbol {Q} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm {T}} \boldsymbol {Q} _ {1}\right) = \det \left( \begin{array}{c c} (\lambda_ {1} - \lambda) & \dots \\ 0 & (\boldsymbol {A} _ {2} - \lambda \boldsymbol {I}) \end{array} \right) \\ = \left(\lambda_ {1} - \lambda\right) \det \left(\boldsymbol {A} _ {2} - \lambda \boldsymbol {I}\right). \\ \end{array}
$$

(2)

So $A_{2}$ has real eigenvalues, namely $\lambda_{2},\dots,\lambda_{n}$ . Now we proceed by induction. Suppose we have proved the theorem for n=k. Then we use this fact to prove the theorem is true for n=k+1 . Note that the theorem is trivial if n=1.

So for $n=k+1$ , we proceed as above and then apply the known theorem to $A_{2}$ , which is $k\times k$ . We find that $A_{2}=Q_{2} T_{2} Q_{2}^{\mathrm{T}}$ . Now this is the hard part. Let $Q_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ be as above, and let

(3)

(3)

$$
Q = Q _ {1} \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & Q _ {2} \end{array} \right)
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} A Q = A Q _ {1} \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & Q _ {2} \end{array} \right) = Q _ {1} \left( \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & \dots \\ 0 & A _ {2} \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & Q _ {2} \end{array} \right) \\ = Q _ {1} \left( \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & \dots \\ 0 & A _ {2} Q _ {2} \end{array} \right) = Q _ {1} \left( \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & \dots \\ 0 & Q _ {2} T _ {2} \end{array} \right) \\ = Q _ {1} \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & Q _ {2} \end{array} \right) \left( \begin{array}{c c} \lambda_ {1} & \dots \\ 0 & T _ {2} \end{array} \right) = Q T, \\ \end{array}
$$

(4)

where $T$ is upper triangular. So $A Q = Q T$, or $A = Q T Q^{\mathrm{T}}$.

That's all, folks!
